title: Maps and directions: how to draw your home so someone else can find their way

summary.text: A map is a drawing of a place as if you were looking down on it from above. It does not show colours, smells or sounds, yet it can lead a stranger straight to a hidden coin. It works because it keeps how far apart things are and which way they lie. North, south, east and west are directions fixed to the Earth, so they mean the same for everyone, whichever way they face. You can find east from the morning Sun, and draw a map of your room by counting floor tiles.
summary.art: A child's squared-paper map of a bedroom, with a bed, a cupboard and a door drawn from above, a small X in the middle of the floor, and an arrow marked N in the corner.

intro.hook: Put a coin on the floor of a room. Can you draw a map so good that someone who did not see you can walk in and put a finger on the coin?
intro.text: In this unit you draw maps of your room, your home and your street. You find out which way north, south, east and west are in your own flat. You test two maps against each other to see which one finds a hidden coin. And you find out how a desert ant finds her way home by counting her steps.
intro.art: A grandmother standing in a doorway holding a small paper map, looking at a coin on a tiled floor, while a girl watches from behind the door.

outcomes: I can name the four directions, north, south, east and west, and find east and north in my home from the morning Sun or a compass.
I can explain why north, south, east and west work for anyone, while left and right change when a person turns.
I can draw a room from above, with a key of symbols and an arrow that shows north.
I can make a map that keeps distances right by counting tiles or steps, and say why that helps someone find a place.
I can turn a map so that it lines up with the room or street I am standing in.
I can read a simple map and give directions from one place to another.
I can tell how people found out that California is not an island, and how a desert ant finds her way home.

explanations.definition: A map is a drawing of a place from above, made smaller, that shows where things are and how far apart they are.
explanations.description: A photo shows a room from the side, the way your eyes see it. A map shows it from straight above. From above, a bed is a rectangle, a round table is a circle, and a door is a gap in a wall. A map also leaves things out. It does not show the colour of the curtains or the smell from the kitchen. It keeps only what helps someone find their way: what is where, how far apart things are, and which way they lie. That is why a map can be far simpler than a photo and still be more useful for finding a place.
examples: A map of a school shows each classroom as a box with its number.
A bus route map in Bengaluru shows the stops as dots on a line, and leaves out the houses.
The map on a phone shows roads as lines and the place you are as a blue dot.
explanations.art: On the left, a photo-like drawing of a room from the side. On the right, the same room as a map from above.
explanations.context: This card explains what makes a drawing a map, and why a map leaves so much out.

explanations.definition: North, south, east and west are four directions fixed to the Earth. North points towards the North Pole, south towards the South Pole. East is where the Sun rises, roughly, and west is where it sets.
explanations.description: The Earth spins like a top. The two ends of the line it spins round are the North Pole and the South Pole. North is the direction towards the North Pole, from wherever you are. South is the opposite. The Earth spins towards the east, so every morning the Sun comes up roughly in the east, and every evening it goes down roughly in the west. In India, the place where the Sun rises shifts a little through the year. It rises a little north of east in June, and a little south of east in December. Between the four main directions are four more: north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west.
examples: Kanyakumari is at the southern tip of mainland India.
Delhi is north of Chennai.
Bengaluru is west of Chennai.
explanations.art: A globe with the North Pole at the top and an arrow from India pointing to it, and a small Sun rising on the eastern edge.
explanations.context: This card explains what the four directions are, and why the Sun rises in the east.

explanations.concept: Finding the directions in your own home
explanations.definition: In the morning, the Sun is roughly in the east. Stand with your right hand towards it, and you are facing north.
explanations.description: You do not need to go outside. Look at which window gets the Sun early in the morning, between about 7 and 9 o'clock. That side of your flat faces roughly east. Stand with your right arm pointing to that window. Now you are facing north. East is on your right, west is on your left, and south is behind you. A compass gives the same answer at any time of day. Its needle is a small magnet that turns to point north and south. Many phones have a compass app too. Never look straight at the Sun to find it. Look at where its light falls.
examples: In a Chennai flat, the balcony that gets the morning Sun faces east, towards the Bay of Bengal.
The window that gets the red evening Sun faces roughly west.
A compass on a table points north whichever way you turn the table.
explanations.art: A child in a living room with the right arm pointing at a sunny window and facing a wall labelled N.
explanations.context: This card tells you how to find north, south, east and west inside your flat, without going out.

explanations.concept: Left and right, or north and south?
explanations.definition: Left, right, forward and back belong to your body, so they change whenever you turn. North, south, east and west belong to the Earth, so they stay the same whichever way you face.
explanations.description: Say a friend is told, "Walk three tiles forward, then turn right." Where she ends up depends on which way she was facing when she began. If she starts facing a different wall, she ends up in a different place. Now say she is told, "Walk three tiles towards the east wall, then two tiles towards the south wall." She ends up in the same place whichever way she started. That is why maps use north, south, east and west. A map is read by many people, each standing a different way. Left and right are still useful when you walk with someone, because you both face the same way.
examples: A sailor at sea says the ship is heading north-east, not left.
In the Guugu Yimithirr language of north-east Australia, people say "the cup is north of the plate" instead of left or right.
Bus drivers in a city still say "take the second left", because they know which way you face.
explanations.art: Two girls on the same tile, facing different walls, with dotted arrows showing that 'forward then right' leads them to different places.
explanations.context: This card explains why maps use north, south, east and west instead of left and right.

explanations.concept: Symbols, a key and a north arrow
explanations.definition: A map uses symbols for real things, a key to say what each symbol means, and an arrow or compass rose to show which way is north.
explanations.description: Drawing every leaf of a tree would take hours, so a map uses a symbol, such as a small circle. The key in one corner lists every symbol and its meaning, so any reader can understand them. The north arrow tells the reader how to turn the map. Hold the map so its north arrow points to the real north. Now everything on the map lies the same way as the real things around you. This is called setting, or turning, the map. Most maps put north at the top, but that is only a custom. Al-Idrisi, a mapmaker in Sicily, drew a famous map of the world in 1154 with south at the top.
examples: On Indian railway maps, a small train symbol often marks a station.
On a map of a temple, a small drawn tower can mark each gopuram.
In a phone map, the blue dot is a symbol for you.
explanations.art: A hand-drawn map of a flat with a key box listing a door, a window, a bed and a tap, and an N arrow.
explanations.context: This card is about the three things that make a map easy for anyone to read.

explanations.definition: Scale is how much smaller a map is than the real place. On a good map, every distance is shrunk by the same amount.
explanations.description: Many Indian flats have square floor tiles. If you draw one square on squared paper for each tile, the room on paper is smaller, but every distance shrinks by the same amount. A bed four tiles long becomes four squares long. A gap of two tiles becomes two squares. So the shape of the room stays right. If a map shrinks some things more than others, the shape goes wrong, and a reader looking for a spot will miss it. With no tiles, you can count your own steps, heel to toe.
examples: A tile map: one square on paper stands for one floor tile.
A map of India in an atlas may say 1 centimetre stands for 100 kilometres.
Nain Singh Rawat mapped the road to Lhasa by counting his steps on a string of 100 beads.
explanations.art: A tiled floor with a bed and a cupboard, and next to it a squared-paper map where each tile is one square.
explanations.context: This card explains scale, and why counting tiles makes a map that someone else can trust.

explanations.concept: How a desert ant finds her way home
explanations.definition: A desert ant finds her way home by keeping track of her direction, using the Sun, and of how far she has walked, by counting her steps.
explanations.description: Cataglyphis ants live in the Sahara desert, where the ground can be hotter than 50 degrees. A worker ant must go far from her nest alone to find dead insects to eat, and get back fast before the heat kills her. Smell trails do not help much on hot, windy sand. So the ant keeps track of two things. She uses the Sun to know which way she is going. And she counts her steps to know how far she has gone. Then she runs straight home. In 2006, scientists in Germany and Switzerland gave some ants tiny stilts. Those ants walked past their nest, because their longer steps carried them further than they had counted.
examples: An ant with stilts overshot her nest.
An ant with shortened legs stopped before she reached her nest.
Both results show the ant was counting steps, not just looking for her nest.
explanations.art: A desert ant running across pale sand under a bright Sun, with a dotted zigzag path out and a straight path back to a small nest hole.
explanations.context: This card is about a desert ant, and how she finds her way home with no map at all.

agreed.text: North, south, east and west are fixed to the Earth. North points towards the North Pole.
agreed.evidence: A compass needle points the same way whichever way you turn its box, and sailors and pilots everywhere use the same directions.

agreed.text: The Sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west, because the Earth spins towards the east.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can watch which window gets the morning Sun and which gets the evening Sun, every day of the year.

agreed.text: A map that keeps all distances shrunk by the same amount lets a reader find places on the real ground.
agreed.evidence: A tile map, with one square for each floor tile, leads a reader to the right tile. Surveyors map whole countries the same way, by measuring.

agreed.text: Maps can be wrong, and the only way to check a map is to compare it with the real place.
agreed.evidence: For about a hundred years, European maps showed California as an island, until travellers walked round the top of the gulf.

agreed.text: Many animals find their way without maps, using the Sun, smells, landmarks and counting steps.
agreed.evidence: Desert ants on stilts walked past their nest, which shows they measure distance by counting steps.

challenging.claim: North is up, towards the sky.
challenging.who: A common idea among children, because maps on a wall have north at the top
challenging.for: On most maps, north is at the top, and wall maps hang with the top up.
challenging.against: North is a direction along the ground, towards the North Pole. Lay a map flat on the floor, turn it to match the room, and north points to a wall, not the ceiling.
challenging.context: This card is about a mix-up between the top of a map and the direction north.

challenging.claim: The Sun rises exactly in the east every day.
challenging.for: The Sun always rises on the eastern side, so it is a fine rule for finding east.
challenging.against: In India, the Sun rises a little north of east in June and a little south of east in December. It rises exactly east only around 20 March and 23 September.
challenging.context: This card is about how exact the rule 'the Sun rises in the east' is.

challenging.claim: A good map shows everything in a place.
challenging.who: A common first idea when children draw maps
challenging.for: A map with more things on it seems to tell you more.
challenging.against: A map with everything on it would be crowded and hard to read. A good map shows what the reader needs, and a key explains it.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a map should show everything.

challenging.claim: A compass needle points exactly to the North Pole.
challenging.for: A compass does point roughly north everywhere in India.
challenging.against: The needle points to the magnetic north pole, which is some distance from the North Pole and slowly moves. In India the difference is small, so a compass is good enough for a home map.
challenging.context: This card is about how exact a compass is.

big_questions.q: Your tile map had no colours and no cushions on it, yet it found the coin. What does a map need to keep to be true?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you left out, and what you were careful to get right.

big_questions.q: If you walk north and keep going, where do you end up? And which way is south from there?
big_questions.hint: Think about the North Pole. From there, every direction leads away from it.

big_questions.q: A desert ant counts her steps with no paper and no numbers. Is she making a map?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a map does for you, and whether the ant does the same thing inside her body.

big_questions.q: Borders between countries are drawn on maps, but you cannot see them on the ground. Are they real?
big_questions.hint: Think about who drew them, and what changes when people agree on them.

big_questions.q: Your brain keeps a map of your home, so you can walk to the kitchen in the dark. Where is that map?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you know where the door is with your eyes closed.

story.title: Thatha and the Six Towers
story.note: The story is made up. Everything about the map is true: a map works when it is turned to match the ground, and when its distances are counted, not guessed.
text: Meenakshi's Thatha came to stay in the summer holidays. He had lived all his life in a village near Tirunelveli, where every lane had a name he knew and every neighbour knew him. Now he was in Chennai, in a flat on the fifth floor of Tower D.
There were six towers in the complex, A to F. They were all the same height and the same cream colour, with the same blue railings on every balcony.

On the first morning, Thatha went down to buy milk from the booth at the gate. He did not come back for an hour. When he finally rang the bell, his forehead was wet and he was holding the milk packet very tightly.
"I went into Tower B," he said. "Then Tower E. Every tower looks the same. Every lift looks the same. A watchman had to bring me here."
Meenakshi was eight, and she was good at drawing. "I will make you a map, Thatha," she said.

She sat at the dining table and drew six boxes for the six towers. She drew the gate and the milk booth. She drew the round water tank and the small Pillaiyar temple near the gate. She wrote D in big letters on their tower and drew a star on it.
The next morning, Thatha went down with the map in his shirt pocket. This time he was gone for forty minutes.
"Your map is beautiful, kanna," he said, sitting down heavily. "But when I came out of the milk booth, the temple was on my left. On your map it was on the right. So I walked the wrong way."

Meenakshi looked at the map. She had drawn the gate at the bottom of the page. But Thatha had come back in from the gate, facing the towers. When he held the map with the gate at the bottom, he was fine. When he turned round, the map did not turn with him.
"Left and right change when you turn," she said slowly. "I need something on the map that does not change."
Her mother was cutting vegetables in the kitchen. "What about the Sun?" she said. "In the morning, our kitchen window is full of sunlight. That side faces east."

So Meenakshi stood at the kitchen window. The Sun was pouring in over the towers, so she looked at the patch of light on the floor, not at the Sun. Then she went back to her map. She worked out where their kitchen was on Tower D, and which side of the complex was the sunny side. She drew a big arrow on the map and wrote E at its tip. Then she drew a cross with N, S, E and W.

"Thatha," she said, "tomorrow, when you come out of the milk booth, look for the Sun. Turn the map until the E arrow points at the sunny side. Then everything on the map will be on the same side as the real thing."

The next morning, Thatha was back in twenty minutes. "The arrow worked," he said. "I turned the map, and the temple was on the same side as on the paper. But then I walked too far. On your map, Tower D is right next to the water tank. In real life it is much further."
Meenakshi frowned. She had drawn the water tank as big as a tower, and squeezed the towers close together so they would fit on the page. She had guessed every distance.

That evening, she and her mother walked from the gate to Tower D. Meenakshi counted her steps. From the gate to the temple was 20 steps. From the temple to the water tank was 60 steps. From the water tank to Tower D was 90 steps. She wrote every number in her notebook.

At home, she drew a new map on squared paper from her maths notebook. One square was ten of her steps. The temple was 2 squares from the gate. The water tank was 6 squares further. Tower D was 9 squares beyond that. Now the map looked strange. The towers were small, and there was a lot of empty paper between them. But every gap was the right size compared with every other gap.
"It looks emptier," said her mother.
"It is more true," said Meenakshi.

On the fourth morning, Thatha came out of the milk booth. He found the Sun, turned the map until the E arrow pointed at it, and set off. Past the temple. A long walk to the water tank, just as long as on the map. Then a longer walk to the tower with the star. He rang the bell after nine minutes, and he was smiling.
"I did not need the watchman today," he said. He took a pencil from his pocket and drew a small circle on the map, on the path between the water tank and Tower D.
"What is that?" asked Meenakshi.
"The neem tree with the bench in the shade," said Thatha. "Tomorrow, I am going to sit there and read the newspaper. Now I know how to get back."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenakshi's first map failed twice for two different reasons. First, it used left and right, which change when the reader turns. An east arrow fixed that, because east is the same for everyone, and the reader can turn the map to match the ground. Second, the distances were guessed, so they were out of proportion. Counting steps fixed that, because every distance was shrunk by the same amount. A map that is turned the right way and has true distances can guide someone who has never been there.
ask: Why did Thatha walk the wrong way the second morning, even with the map?
How did the E arrow help him, and how did Meenakshi find which way east was?
Why did the counted map look emptier than the first one?
Thatha added a neem tree to the map. What would you add to a map of your building?

games.title: Vadakku, Therku! A turn-and-face direction game
games.context: This is a quick game in one room. A caller says a direction in English, Tamil, Malayalam, Telugu or Hindi, and everyone turns to face it as fast as they can.
rules: Stick the four wall labels on the right walls first. Use the morning Sun or a compass to find them.
Shuffle the direction cards and put them face down. One player is the caller.
The caller reads a card aloud. Everyone else turns to face that direction and points.
Anyone facing the right wall scores 1. The last one to turn, or anyone facing the wrong wall, scores 0.
After 4 cards, take the wall labels down. Now you must remember the directions.
After 8 cards, the caller says two directions, such as 'between north and east'. Point to the corner.
Swap callers after every 8 cards. The player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Stick the N, S, E and W labels on the walls. 2. Cut out the cards. 3. Choose a caller.
flow.say: First we put up the four labels. Each one shows a direction. Then we take turns calling.
flow.kid: Put the four labels on the walls. Choose who calls first.
flow.context: This is the first step of a turn-and-face game about the four directions.

flow.do: 1. The caller reads cards one by one. 2. Players turn and point. 3. Keep score. 4. After 4 cards, take the labels down.
flow.say: Kizhakku! Which way is that? Turn and point. Now the labels come down. Can you still find north?
flow.kid: Listen. Turn and point. Can you do it with no labels?
flow.parent: If your child gets stuck once the labels are down, ask: where was the sunny window this morning? That side is east.

flow.do: Call two directions at once, for example 'between south and west'.
flow.say: Between south and west. Point to that corner. What do we call that direction?
flow.kid: Point between south and west. What is its name?

check.q: You face north. Which direction is behind you?
check.why: South is always opposite north. If you face north, south is behind you, east is on your right and west is on your left. Picking east or west means you turned only halfway round.

flow.do: Talk about the game.
flow.say: When you turned round, did the north wall move? What changed, and what stayed the same?
flow.kid: When you turned, did north move?
flow.think: Your right hand pointed at a different wall each time. Did north ever change?

games.title: Tile Treasure: a grid treasure-hunt board game
games.context: This is a board game on a printed grid map of a flat. Players move their token with direction cards, such as '2 squares east', to collect coins hidden in the rooms.

printables.title: A grid map of a flat, 10 squares by 8
items: A grid of 80 squares with a north arrow at the top
Rooms drawn on the grid: kitchen, hall, two bedrooms, bathroom and balcony, with doors as gaps
Eight coin spots marked with a small circle: the fridge, the TV, the pooja shelf, a bed, the balcony plant, the washing machine, the shoe rack and the dining table
A start square at the front door

printables.title: Tokens
items: 4 player tokens: use a button, a bindi packet, a bottle cap or a coin

rules: Put all tokens on the start square at the front door. Put a paper coin on each coin spot.
Each player holds 3 direction cards. Put the rest face down.
On your turn, play one card and move your token that many squares in that direction. Then take a new card.
You cannot walk through walls. If a wall blocks you, stop at the wall.
Land on a coin spot to pick up the coin there.
Before you move, say where you will end up. If you are right, score 1 extra point.
When all coins are gone, the player with the most coins and points wins. Playing alone, collect all 8 coins in as few turns as you can.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the board. 2. Put coins on the coin spots. 3. Deal 3 cards each.
flow.say: This is a map of a flat, drawn on squares. North is at the top. Let's find the kitchen and the balcony.
flow.kid: Find north on the board. Find the kitchen and the balcony.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tile Treasure, a board game where you move on a grid map using directions.

flow.do: Play one practice move together.
flow.say: My token is at the door. I play '3 squares east'. Where will I land? Point first, then let's count.
flow.kid: Your token is at the door. You play 3 squares east. Where do you land?

check.q: On the board, north is at the top. Which way is east?
check.why: With north at the top, east is on the right, west on the left and south at the bottom. Picking the left edge is a common mix-up, so say it aloud: never eat soggy wheat, north, east, south, west, going round clockwise.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Say where you will land, then move. 3. Keep score.
flow.say: Say where you will land before you move. A right guess is an extra point.
flow.kid: Say where you will land. Then move. Right guess? Extra point!
flow.parent: Ask your child to give you directions sometimes: 'Tell me how to get from the fridge to the balcony.' A strong answer uses directions and counts, such as '2 squares south, then 4 east'.

flow.do: Talk about the game.
flow.say: If I turned the board round, would '3 squares east' still take you to the same place?
flow.kid: Turn the board round. Does 3 east still go the same place?
flow.think: East on the board is fixed by the north arrow. What happens if someone draws the arrow pointing the other way?

experiments.title: Memory Map or Tile Map: which one finds the hidden coin?
experiments.question: Does a map drawn by counting floor tiles lead someone closer to a hidden coin than a map drawn from memory?
experiments.predict: You will draw two maps of the same room: one from memory, and one by counting tiles. Which one will lead a family member closer to a hidden coin? Or will both be just as good? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same room, the same finder and the same things drawn on both maps. Hide the coin in open floor, at least two tiles away from any furniture, so the finder cannot just look for 'next to the bed'. Use each map twice, taking turns, so that practice does not help one map more than the other. Only the way the map was made changes.

materials.item: a room with square floor tiles, such as a bedroom or the hall. No tiles? Count heel-to-toe steps instead.
two sheets of squared paper, from a maths notebook
a pencil and an eraser
a one-rupee coin
a small paper chit, about the size of a coin
a family member to be the finder

experiments.safety: Clear toys and loose things off the floor first, so no one trips while counting tiles.

schedule.what: Draw a memory map and a tile map of one room. Hide a coin four times and see which map leads the finder closer.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then add up the tiles off for each map. The smaller total is the better map.

flow.do: 1. Sit outside the room, with the door closed. 2. Draw the room from above on the first sheet, from memory. 3. Draw the walls, the door, the window and the big furniture. 4. Do not count anything.
flow.say: First, draw this room from memory, as a bird would see it from the ceiling. Don't go in and look. Just draw what you remember.
flow.kid: Sit outside the room. Draw it from above, from memory. No counting!
flow.parent: Most children draw the furniture too big and the empty floor too small. Do not correct it. That is part of the test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Memory Map or Tile Map test. You draw two maps of one room, then see which one leads someone to a hidden coin.

flow.do: 1. Go into the room. 2. Count the tiles along one long wall and one short wall. 3. On the second sheet, draw the walls with one square for each tile. 4. Count tiles from the walls to each piece of furniture, and draw it the same way.
flow.say: Now we draw a second map of the same room. This time, one tile on the floor is one square on the paper. Count every tile.
flow.kid: Count the tiles along the wall. One tile is one square. Draw each thing where you count it.
flow.parent: Half tiles at the wall edges can be drawn as half squares. Small rooms often have 20 to 40 tiles along a wall if the tiles are small. If your tiles are big, the room may be only 5 or 6 tiles long. Both work.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Which map will lead the finder closer to the coin? Or will they be the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which map will work better? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that map will work better?
good: Because I counted, so the places are right.
Because the memory map has the bed too big.
Because both show the bed and the door, so both will work.

flow.parent: Any reason is fine. Do not say what you expect.

flow.do: 1. The finder waits outside. 2. Your child puts the coin on a tile in open floor, away from furniture. 3. They mark an X on the memory map and secretly write the true spot, as tiles from two walls. 4. They pick up the coin. 5. The finder comes in with the memory map and puts the chit where the X shows. 6. Put the coin back on its true tile and count the tiles between the chit and the coin. 7. Do the same with a new spot and the tile map. 8. Do one more round with each map.
flow.say: Now the finder comes in with only the map. No hints and no pointing. When the chit is down, we count how many tiles off it is.
flow.kid: Hide the coin. Mark an X. Pick the coin up. Let the finder use the map. How many tiles off?
flow.parent: Usually the tile map puts the chit on the right tile or the next one. The memory map is often 2 to 4 tiles off, because some things were drawn too big. If both maps land close, choose a spot further from all furniture and try again.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: What I think: the tile map is better for finding things. What I saw: the tile map was 0 and 1 tiles off, and the memory map was 3 and 2 tiles off. Why: on the tile map, every distance was shrunk by the same amount, so the X was in the right place compared with the walls.

check.q: Why did the tile map lead the finder to the right spot?
options: It had more things drawn on it
Every distance was shrunk by the same amount, so the X sat in the right place
check.why: On the tile map, one tile became one square, so every gap on paper matched the gap on the floor. Picking 'more things' is a fair guess, but both maps showed the same furniture. Neatness helps reading, but a neat map with wrong distances still leads you to the wrong spot.

experiments.context: In this experiment you draw two maps of the same room, one from memory and one by counting tiles. Then you test which one leads a family member closer to a hidden coin.

experiments.title: Left-Right or East-West: which directions still work when you face another way?
experiments.question: If someone starts facing a different way, do 'forward and turn right' directions still lead to the coin? Do 'east and south' directions?
experiments.predict: You will follow two sets of directions to a coin, starting each time facing a different wall. Which set will find the coin every time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Start on the same tile each time, and walk the same number of tiles. Use tiles, not steps, because people's steps are different sizes. Only the way you face at the start changes.

materials.item: the N, S, E and W wall labels, from the Find the Four Directions activity
a room with floor tiles, or a row of newspaper sheets laid in a grid
a cushion or a mat to mark the start tile
a one-rupee coin
two paper chits and a pencil
four small chits marked 'face N', 'face E', 'face S' and 'face W', folded

experiments.safety: Clear the floor first. Walk, don't run, and keep away from sharp corners.

schedule.what: Follow two sets of directions from four different starting directions. Count how often each set finds the coin.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with a tick or a cross. Count the ticks for each set.

flow.do: 1. Put the cushion on a tile. 2. Stand on it facing east, and put the coin 3 tiles forward and 2 tiles to the right. 3. Write chit A: 'Walk 3 tiles forward. Turn right. Walk 2 tiles.' 4. Write chit B: 'Walk 3 tiles towards the east wall. Then walk 2 tiles towards the south wall.'
flow.say: We will write two sets of directions to the same coin. One uses forward and right. The other uses east and south.
flow.kid: Two chits. Both lead to the coin. One says right. One says east and south.
flow.parent: Check the coin's place. Facing east, your right hand points south. So '2 tiles right' and '2 tiles towards the south wall' are the same tiles.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Left-Right or East-West test. You find out which kind of directions still work when someone starts facing another way.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will start facing a different wall each time. Which chit will find the coin every time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which chit will always work? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Many children think both will work, because both were right the first time.

flow.do: 1. Pick a folded 'face' chit. 2. Stand on the cushion facing that wall. 3. Follow chit A and put a finger on the tile where you stop. 4. Go back to the cushion, face the same wall, and follow chit B. 5. Fill in the table. 6. Do all four 'face' chits.
flow.say: Pick a chit to see which wall to face. Follow chit A. Did you land on the coin? Now chit B.
flow.kid: Pick a chit. Face that wall. Follow A. Then follow B. Coin?
flow.parent: Chit B finds the coin all four times. Chit A finds it only when you start facing east, the way the writer faced.

flow.do: Talk about the results.
flow.say: Chit A worked only once. Chit B worked every time. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Chit A worked once. Chit B always worked. Why?

check.q: Why did chit B find the coin from every start?
options: East and south stay the same whichever way you face
Chit B was written more neatly
The coin moved when you turned
check.why: East and south are fixed to the Earth, so the east wall is the east wall whichever way you face. 'Forward' and 'right' turn when your body turns. That is why maps use north, south, east and west.

experiments.context: In this experiment you follow two kinds of directions to a coin, starting each time facing a different wall.

setup.art: A cushion on a tiled floor, a coin three tiles ahead and two to the side, and labels N, E, S and W on the walls.
setup.caption: 1. Put the coin in place and write two chits.

setup.art: A boy standing on the cushion facing the N wall, holding chit A, with a dotted arrow leading away from the coin.
setup.caption: 2. Face a new wall. Follow each chit.

experiments.title: Child Steps, Grown-up Steps: do two maps of one room come out the same shape?
experiments.question: If a child and a grown-up each map the same room using their own steps, will the two maps have the same shape?
experiments.predict: A grown-up's foot is longer than yours. Will a grown-up's map of the room be the same shape as yours, or a different shape? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both people walk heel to toe, with the heel touching the toe each time, along the same two walls. Each person counts twice and takes the closer count. Each map uses one square for one step.

materials.item: a room with a clear path along two walls
two sheets of squared paper
a pencil, scissors and a long ruler or a straight stick

experiments.safety: Walk slowly heel to toe, and hold the wall if you wobble. A grown-up handles the scissors with a younger child.

schedule.what: A child and a grown-up each measure a room in their own steps, draw it, and compare the shapes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Cut out both rectangles and stick them in your notebook, one on top of the other, sharing one corner.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will both measure this room in our own footsteps. My feet are bigger. Will our maps be the same shape? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will the two maps be the same shape? Why do you think so?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Child Steps, Grown-up Steps test. Two people map the same room with their own feet.

flow.do: 1. The child walks heel to toe along the long wall and counts. 2. Then along the short wall. 3. The grown-up does the same. 4. Write all four numbers in the table.
flow.say: Heel touching toe, every step. Count out loud. Then it's my turn.
flow.kid: Walk heel to toe along the wall. Count every step.
flow.parent: Example: a child counts 18 steps by 14, and a grown-up 13 by 10. The numbers are different, but each long wall is about 1 and a third times its short wall.

flow.do: 1. Each person draws their room as a rectangle on squared paper, one square for each step. 2. Cut out both rectangles. 3. Put the small one on the big one, sharing the bottom-left corner. 4. Lay the ruler from that corner through the far corner of the big rectangle.
flow.say: Let's cut out both maps and put one on the other. Does the ruler pass through the corner of the small map too?
flow.kid: Cut out both. Put the small one on the big one. Lay the ruler corner to corner.
flow.parent: If the two shapes are the same, the ruler line passes through the far corner of the small rectangle as well. It will be close, not perfect, because steps are never exactly equal.

flow.do: Talk about the result.
flow.say: Our numbers were different. Is one of our maps wrong?
flow.kid: Your numbers were different. Is one map wrong?

check.q: A child's map of a room is bigger on paper than a grown-up's. Both used one square per step. Why?
options: The child's steps are shorter, so the room took more of them
check.why: Shorter feet need more steps to cross the same room, so the child's map has more squares. But both maps shrink every wall by the same amount, so their shapes match. Both maps are right. Each just uses a different scale.

experiments.context: In this experiment you and a grown-up each measure the same room with your own feet, and find out whether your maps come out the same shape.

setup.art: A small paper rectangle placed on a bigger one at the same corner, with a ruler lying from that corner across both far corners.
setup.caption: 2. Put the maps one on the other. Lay a ruler corner to corner.

activities.title: The View From Above: what do things look like to a bird?

materials.item: a steel tumbler, a book, a plate, a pencil box and a banana
a low table or a stool
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: If your child stands on a chair to look down, a grown-up holds the chair steady.

schedule.what: Look at five things from the side, then from straight above. Draw both views.

activities.record: Draw each thing twice: from the side and from above. Circle the drawing that would go on a map.

flow.do: 1. Put the five things on a low table. 2. Ask your child to sit at table height and draw them as they look from the side.
flow.say: Draw these five things the way you see them now, from the side.
flow.kid: Sit low. Draw the five things as you see them.
flow.context: This is a starting activity for the maps unit. You find out how things look from straight above, which is how a map shows them.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to stand and look straight down at the table. 2. Draw the five things again, from above.
flow.say: Now stand up and look straight down, like a crow on the ceiling. Draw them again. What changed?
flow.kid: Stand up. Look straight down. Draw them again.
flow.parent: From above, the tumbler is a circle, the book a rectangle, the plate a circle, and the banana a curved strip. The tumbler's height disappears.

flow.do: Talk about the two drawings.
flow.say: Which drawing shows how far apart the things are? Which one would help someone find the banana on the table?
flow.kid: Which drawing shows where things are? Why?

check.q: From straight above, what shape is a steel tumbler?
check.why: From above you see only the round rim, so a tumbler looks like a circle. A tall rectangle is how it looks from the side. Maps are drawn from above, so a tumbler on a map is a circle.

flow.think: What would your whole flat look like from straight above?

activities.context: This is a quick starting activity. You look at things from the side and from above, and find out why maps are drawn from above.

setup.caption: 1. Draw the things from the side.

activities.title: Find the Four Directions in Your Flat

materials.item: four paper labels: N, S, E and W
cello tape
a phone with a compass app, or a small compass, if you have one

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, even for a moment. Look only at where its light falls on the floor or the wall.

schedule.what: Find east from the morning Sun or a compass, and put up labels for all four directions.

activities.record: Draw a box for the room, mark which wall is N, S, E and W, and draw the window that gets the morning Sun.

flow.do: 1. In the morning, between about 7 and 9 o'clock, find the window or balcony where sunlight comes in. 2. If it is later in the day, use a compass, or ask the family which side gets the morning Sun.
flow.say: The Sun rises in the east. Where is the morning sunlight coming in? Don't look at the Sun. Look at the patch of light.
flow.kid: Find the sunny window. Don't look at the Sun. Look at its light.
flow.parent: In India the Sun rises a little north or south of east, depending on the month, so this gives you rough east. That is fine for a home map. On a cloudy day, use a compass or a phone compass app.
flow.context: This activity helps you find north, south, east and west in your own flat, using the morning Sun or a compass.

flow.do: 1. Stand in the middle of the room with your right arm pointing to the sunny side. 2. You are now facing north. 3. Stick E on the sunny wall and N on the wall in front. Stick W on your left and S behind you.
flow.say: Point your right arm at the sunny side. That is east. Now you face north. Where are south and west?
flow.kid: Right arm to the sun side. That is east. You face north.
flow.parent: If the walls do not line up exactly with the directions, stick each label on the wall that is closest.

flow.do: 1. Check with a compass if you have one. 2. Go round the flat. Which way does the front door face? Which way does the balcony face?
flow.say: Let's check with the compass. Does the needle agree with our labels? Now, which way does our front door face?
flow.kid: Check with a compass. Which way does the front door face?

check.q: You stand with your right arm pointing east. Which way are you facing?
check.why: With east on your right, you face north, west is on your left and south is behind you. Picking south means you turned the wrong way round. Try it again standing up, with your arm out.

activities.context: In this activity you find east from the morning Sun, then work out north, south and west, and label the walls of a room.

activities.title: Map of Our Home, with a Key

materials.item: a large sheet of paper, or two notebook pages taped together
a pencil, an eraser and colour pencils

schedule.what: Walk through the home, then draw a map of it from above, with symbols, a key and a north arrow.

activities.record: Keep the map. You will use it in the Map for a Visitor project.

flow.do: 1. Walk through the home together. 2. In each room, ask your child which wall is next to which room.
flow.say: Let's walk through our home. Which room is next to the kitchen? Which door leads to the balcony?
flow.kid: Walk through your home. What room is next to what?
flow.context: In this activity you draw a map of your whole home, with symbols and a key.

flow.do: 1. Draw each room as a box, in the right place next to the others. 2. Show doors as gaps. 3. Draw small symbols for a few things: the fridge, beds, taps, the pooja shelf, the TV.
flow.say: Draw each room as a box. Make the big rooms bigger. Leave a gap where each door is.
flow.kid: Draw each room as a box. Doors are gaps.
flow.parent: Help your child keep the rooms in the right order. Exact sizes do not matter here. The tile map in the experiment is for exact sizes.

flow.do: 1. Make a key box in one corner. 2. Draw each symbol in the key and write what it means. 3. Draw a north arrow, using the labels from the Find the Four Directions activity.
flow.say: Now the key. Draw every symbol again in this box, and write what it means. Then add the north arrow.
flow.kid: Make a key. What does each symbol mean? Add a north arrow.

flow.do: Test the map on someone.
flow.say: Give the map to Amma. Can she find the pooja shelf using only the map and the key?
flow.kid: Can someone find a thing using only your map?

check.q: What is a key on a map for?
options: To say what each symbol means
check.why: A key lists the symbols and says what each stands for, so any reader can understand the map. The north arrow is a separate thing that shows the way north.

activities.context: In this activity you draw a map of your home from above, with symbols, a key and a north arrow.

activities.title: Directions in Our Languages

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a phone, to call a grandparent or a neighbour, if you like

schedule.what: Learn the four directions in the languages your family speaks, and find a place in India in each direction from your city.

activities.record: Write a table: English, and the words in one or two other languages. Add one place in India in each direction from your city.

flow.do: 1. Read the words below together. 2. Ask grandparents or neighbours for the words in your family's languages. Tamil: vadakku (north), therku (south), kizhakku (east), merku (west). Malayalam: vadakku, thekku, kizhakku, padinjaru. Hindi: uttar, dakshin, purab, paschim.
flow.say: In Tamil, east is kizhakku. In Hindi it is purab. What do we call east at home?
flow.kid: Learn the four directions in another language.
flow.context: In this activity you learn the four directions in Indian languages, and find places in India in each direction.

flow.do: 1. Look at a map of India together, on paper or a phone. 2. Find your city. 3. Name one place to the north, south, east and west of it.
flow.say: Find our city on the map. What is to the south of us? What is to the east?
flow.kid: Find your city. What is north of it? What is south?

check.q: Kanyakumari is at the southern tip of mainland India. Which direction is Kanyakumari from Chennai?
check.why: Kanyakumari is the furthest south of mainland India, so it is south of Chennai, and of every other big city in India.

activities.context: In this activity you learn the four directions in Indian languages, and use a map of India to find places in each direction.

activities.title: The Street from the Balcony

materials.item: a notebook, a pencil and a clipboard or a hardbound book to lean on

activities.safety: A grown-up stays on the balcony. The child stays well away from the railing edge and never climbs on anything.

schedule.what: Look down at the street from a balcony or window and draw it as a map.

activities.record: Draw the street from above, with the road, buildings, trees and shops. Add a north arrow and a key.

flow.do: 1. Go to a balcony or a window that looks over the street. 2. Ask what your child can see: the road, other buildings, trees, a shop, a temple, parked vehicles.
flow.say: Look down at the street. What can you see? Which things will still be there tomorrow?
flow.kid: Look down. What do you see? What stays there every day?
flow.context: In this activity you draw a map of your street from a balcony or a window, the way a bird would see it.

flow.do: 1. Draw the road as two long lines. 2. Draw the buildings as boxes and trees as circles. 3. Leave out things that move, such as autos, cows and people.
flow.say: Draw the road first. Then the buildings as boxes and the trees as circles. Do we draw the autos?
flow.kid: Draw the road. Draw buildings as boxes. Trees as circles.
flow.parent: Things that move are left off maps, because they will not be there tomorrow. Landmarks that stay, such as a temple or a big tree, matter most.

flow.do: 1. Add a north arrow. 2. Add a key.
flow.say: Which way does the street run? From north to south, or from east to west?
flow.kid: Add a north arrow and a key.

check.q: Why do we leave the parked autos off a street map?
options: They are too hard to draw
They move, so they will not be there tomorrow
Autos are not allowed on maps
check.why: A map shows things that stay, so it is still right tomorrow. An auto may be gone in five minutes. A temple or a big tree is a good landmark, because they stay in one place.

activities.context: In this activity you draw your street from above, from a balcony or a window.

activities.title: Turn the Map: make the map match the room

materials.item: the map of your home from the Map of Our Home activity, with its north arrow
the wall labels from the Find the Four Directions activity

schedule.what: Hold the map in different rooms and turn it until its north arrow points to the real north.

activities.record: Write one sentence: what happens to the rooms on the map when its arrow points the real north?

flow.do: 1. Stand in the hall holding the map with the writing the right way up. 2. Point to the kitchen on the map, then to the real kitchen. 3. Now turn the map until its N arrow points to the N wall. 4. Point again.
flow.say: Point to the kitchen on the map. Now point to the real kitchen. Same way? Now turn the map until its arrow points north.
flow.kid: Point to the kitchen on the map. Now to the real one.
flow.context: In this activity you learn to turn a map so that it lines up with the place you are standing in.

flow.do: Go to another room and do it again.
flow.say: Now we are in the bedroom. Turn the map until the arrow points north. Where is the balcony?
flow.kid: In another room, turn the map. Where is the balcony?

check.q: Meera holds a map. The map's north arrow points to her left, but real north is in front of her. What should she do?
options: Turn the map until its arrow points in front of her
Turn herself to face the left
check.why: She turns the map until its north arrow points to the real north. Then every place on the map lies in the same direction as the real place. Turning herself does not help, because the map turns with her.

activities.context: In this activity you turn a map until it lines up with the real room, and see why the north arrow matters.

projects.title: A Map for a Visitor: from the gate to our front door

materials.item: a large sheet of paper or squared paper
a notebook and pencil for counting steps
colour pencils
your wall labels or a compass, to find north

projects.safety: A grown-up walks with the child the whole time outside the flat. Stay on footpaths and away from moving vehicles in the parking area.

schedule.what: Walk from the main gate to your front door with a grown-up. Count steps between landmarks and note the turns.
Draw the route as a map, with one square for every 10 steps, a key and a north arrow.
Give the map to someone who has not walked the route, and walk behind them as they follow it.

projects.record: Keep the counting notes and the map. After the test, write what the visitor found hard, and one change you made.

flow.do: 1. Start at the main gate of your building or complex. 2. Walk to your front door. 3. Count steps between landmarks: the gate, the watchman's cabin, a tree, the lift, the stairs. 4. Write each count and each turn.
flow.say: We will walk from the gate to our door. Count your steps out loud between each landmark. I will write them down.
flow.kid: Walk from the gate. Count steps between landmarks.
flow.context: This is the first day of a 3-day project. You make a map that a visitor could use to find your front door.

flow.do: 1. Draw the route on squared paper, with one square for every 10 steps. 2. Draw each landmark with a symbol. 3. Add a key, a north arrow and the floor number.
flow.say: Now we draw it. Ten steps is one square. Where does the path turn? Which way is north?
flow.kid: Draw the route. Ten steps is one square. Add a key and a north arrow.
flow.parent: Round the counts to the nearest 10. For example, 47 steps is about 5 squares. If there is a lift, write the floor number in a box at the lift.

flow.do: 1. Give the map to someone who has not walked the route, such as a cousin, an aunt or a neighbour. 2. Walk behind them without helping. 3. Note where they stop or go wrong.
flow.say: Let's see if your map works. I will not help. Watch where she gets stuck.
flow.kid: Give your map to a visitor. Don't help! Where did she get stuck?

check.q: Your visitor got lost at the lift, because two lifts were side by side. What is the best fix for your map?
options: Add a symbol for each lift and mark which one to take
Remove the lift from the map
check.why: The visitor needs to know which lift to take, so the map should show both lifts and mark the right one. A bigger map without that detail would leave the same problem.

projects.context: In this project you make a map that a visitor can follow from your building's gate to your front door, and test it on a real person.

challenges.title: A Map with No Words
challenges.problem: Make a map of your home that leads a person to the fridge, the balcony and the bathroom, without a single written word. Someone who cannot read your language must be able to use it.
constraints: No letters or words anywhere on the map, not even in the key.
The map must still show which way north is.
Test it on someone and change it if they get stuck.
materials: paper, a pencil and colour pencils
general: Use pictures as symbols: a small drawing of a fridge, a plant pot for the balcony, a tap for the bathroom.
Show north with a picture of a rising Sun on the east side instead of the letter N.
creative: Use colours as a code: blue for water places, green for plants, yellow for light.
Draw footprints along the route, and a big dot where the walk begins.
Draw each door as the shape of the real door handle.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own wordless map of a place you know well, such as a temple, a park or your grandparents' home, and test it on someone.

flow.do: Read the problem and talk about how to show things without words.
flow.say: No words at all. How can we show the fridge? How can we show which way is east?
flow.kid: No words! How will you show the fridge? And east?
flow.context: This is a design challenge. You make a map that works without any words, so anyone can use it.

flow.do: 1. Draw the rooms. 2. Draw a picture symbol for each place. 3. Show the east side with a rising Sun. 4. Draw the route from the front door.
flow.say: Draw the rooms and the picture symbols. How will the reader know which way to turn the map?
flow.kid: Draw the rooms. Draw picture symbols. Show the east side.

flow.do: 1. Test the map on someone. 2. Read the usual and creative ideas. 3. Improve the map.
flow.say: Let's test it. Then look at the other ideas. Would any make your map better?
flow.kid: Test it. Then try another idea.

check.q: Why does a wordless map still need something that shows a direction, like a rising Sun on the east side?
options: So the reader can turn the map to match the real place
Because all maps must have a Sun
check.why: Without a direction, the reader cannot tell which way to hold the map, and left and right will be wrong when they turn. A rising Sun on the east side tells them how to turn it.

challenges.title: Steer the Toy Car: directions on a tile grid
challenges.problem: Write the shortest set of direction instructions that moves a toy car from one corner of a tiled room to a coin, going round two obstacles. Use only directions and numbers, such as '3 tiles east'.
constraints: Only north, south, east and west, and numbers of tiles. No left or right.
The car moves one tile at a time and cannot pass through an obstacle.
Someone else must follow your instructions without your help.
materials: a small toy car, or a steel katori to slide
two cushions or chairs as obstacles
the N, S, E and W wall labels
general: Draw the room as a grid first, with the car, the obstacles and the coin, then plan the route on paper.
Count each straight stretch and write it as one instruction.
creative: Find two different routes and see which has fewer instructions.
Add a 'fuel' rule: each instruction costs one coin, so the cheapest route wins.
Swap roles: let your parent write the route and you follow it.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own obstacle course and challenge your family to write the shortest route.

flow.do: 1. Put the car on a corner tile, the coin on another tile, and two obstacles between them. 2. Draw the room as a grid on paper.
flow.say: Here is the car, here is the coin. Draw a grid of the floor with everything on it.
flow.kid: Draw the floor as a grid. Mark the car, the coin and the cushions.
flow.context: This is a design challenge. You write directions that steer a toy car round obstacles to a coin.

flow.do: 1. Plan the route on the grid. 2. Write it as instructions, such as '4 tiles north, 2 tiles east'. 3. Count the instructions.
flow.say: Plan the route on paper. How few instructions can you use?
flow.kid: Plan a route. Write it as tiles and directions.

flow.do: 1. Give the instructions to someone else. 2. They move the car without your help. 3. Did it reach the coin? Read the other ideas and improve the route.
flow.say: Hand over your instructions. No helping! Did the car reach the coin?
flow.kid: Give your route to someone. No helping. Did it work?

check.q: A route says '2 tiles north, 3 tiles east, 2 tiles south'. Which shorter route reaches the same tile?
check.why: Going 2 north and then 2 south cancels out, so the car ends just 3 tiles east of where it began. It goes the long way round only if something is in the way.

quiz.p: You stand in your room with your right arm pointing at the window that gets the morning Sun. Which way are you facing?
quiz.why: The morning Sun is roughly in the east, so your right arm points east. With east on your right, you face north. Picking east means you named the arm's direction, not the way you face.

quiz.p: Which tells you where east is, roughly, inside a flat?
opts: The window that gets the evening Sun
The window that gets the morning Sun
quiz.why: The Sun rises roughly in the east, so the window with morning sunlight faces roughly east. The evening Sun comes in from the west.

quiz.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3, gives her friend directions to a hidden coin: 'Walk 3 tiles forward, then turn right.' Her friend starts facing a different wall. What happens?
opts: She ends up in a different place
quiz.why: Forward and right depend on which way you face. A different start means a different path. Directions like 'towards the east wall' work from any start.

quiz.p: Why do maps use north, south, east and west instead of left and right?
opts: They stay the same whichever way a reader faces
Left and right are only for roads
quiz.why: Every reader of a map faces a different way. North, south, east and west are fixed to the Earth, so they mean the same to all of them.

quiz.p: From straight above, what does a round dining table look like on a map?
quiz.why: From above you see only the round top, so it is a circle. The legs are hidden under it. Maps draw things as they look from above.

quiz.p: Pooja, a girl in Class 3, draws a small blue circle on her map for the water tank. Where should she say what the blue circle means?
quiz.why: The key lists every symbol and its meaning, so a reader who has never seen the map before can understand it.

quiz.p: Arun, a boy in Class 3, made a tile map with one square for each floor tile. His bed is 5 tiles long. How long is the bed on his map?
quiz.why: One tile is one square, so 5 tiles is 5 squares. Every distance shrinks by the same amount, which keeps the shape of the room right.

quiz.p: In the coin test, the memory map led the finder 3 tiles away from the coin. The tile map led her to the right tile. Why?
opts: The tile map had more furniture
On the tile map, every gap was the right size compared with the others
quiz.why: Counting tiles kept every distance in the same proportion, so the X was in the right place. On the memory map, some things were drawn too big, so the X was off.

quiz.p: A map's north arrow points to the top of the page. Real north is on your right. How should you hold the map?
opts: Turn it until its top points to your right
Hold it with the top away from you
quiz.why: Turn the map until its north arrow points to real north. Then everything on the map lies the same way as the real places.

quiz.p: On a map with north at the top, the school is directly above your house. Which way do you walk from your house to the school?
quiz.why: Up the page is north on this map, so the school is north of your house.

quiz.p: Before about 1700, many European maps showed California as an island. How was this shown to be wrong?
opts: Travellers went there and saw the land was joined to the mainland
quiz.why: Eusebio Kino travelled over land and saw that there was no sea between California and the mainland. A map is checked by comparing it with the real place.

quiz.p: Scientists gave desert ants tiny stilts. The ants walked past their nest. What does this show?
opts: The ants count their steps to know how far they have gone
quiz.why: Longer legs made longer steps. The ants walked their usual number of steps, which carried them too far. So they were counting steps to measure distance.

items.p: The Sun rises roughly in the ____.
items.why: The Earth spins towards the east, so the Sun comes up on the eastern side every morning.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a drawing of a place from above
a small mark that stands for a real thing
a tool whose needle points north
something easy to see that helps you find your way
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words come up all through the unit.

items.p: You face north. Which direction is on your right?
items.why: Facing north, east is on your right and west on your left. Stand up and try it with the wall labels.

items.p: Draw a steel plate, a pencil and a cup on a table, as a bird would see them from straight above.
items.a: A circle for the plate, a long thin rectangle for the pencil, and a smaller circle for the cup.
items.why: A strong drawing shows only the shapes you see from above, with no sides or legs.

items.p: On a map, things that move, such as autos and cows, are usually left out.
items.why: True. A map should still be right tomorrow, so it shows things that stay, such as roads, buildings and big trees.

items.p: Sort these. Would each one go on a map of your street, or be left off?
items.a: see items
items.why: A map keeps things that stay in one place. A strong sorter asks: will it still be there tomorrow?

items.p: Kavya's right arm points to the window where the morning Sun comes in. Which wall is she facing? Explain how you know.
items.a: She faces the north wall. The morning Sun is in the east, so her right arm points east. When east is on your right, you face north.
items.why: A strong answer starts from the Sun being in the east and works out the rest.

items.p: Why should you never look straight at the Sun to find east?
items.why: Sunlight is strong enough to damage your eyes. Look at where its light falls on the floor or wall instead.

items.p: Put these in order, going clockwise round a compass, starting at north.
items.why: Clockwise from north: north, east, south, west. Some children remember it as 'never eat soggy wheat'.

items.p: In the coin test, which map led the finder closer to the coin: the memory map or the tile map? Use your own numbers to explain.
items.a: The tile map. For example: the tile map was 0 and 1 tiles off, and the memory map was 3 and 2 tiles off. On the tile map I counted, so every distance was right compared with the others.
items.why: A strong answer gives the result, the numbers as evidence, and the reason: counting kept the distances in proportion.

items.p: On a tile map, one floor tile is drawn as one ____ on the paper.
items.why: One tile, one square. That keeps every distance shrunk by the same amount.

items.p: 'Turn left at the door' means the same thing for everyone, whichever way they face.
items.why: False. Left depends on which way you face. Someone coming in from the other side turns the other way.

items.p: Here is a cross for a compass. Write N, S, E and W at its four ends. North is at the top.
items.a: N at the top, S at the bottom, E on the right, W on the left.
items.why: With north at the top, east is on the right. A strong answer checks it by facing north and pointing right.
items.art: A plain cross with four empty boxes at its ends.

items.p: Leela, a girl in Class 3, is drawing a map of her home. What should she draw to show which way north is?
items.why: A north arrow, or a compass rose, shows which way north is. The key explains the symbols.

items.p: Your aunt has never been to your flat. Write directions from the lift to your front door, using at least one direction word such as east or north.
items.a: Any clear directions with landmarks and counts. For example: Come out of the lift and walk east along the corridor, towards the window. Ours is the third door on the north side, with a kolam outside.
items.why: A strong answer uses landmarks, counts and at least one direction word, so it works whichever way the aunt faces.

items.p: Two sisters are giving directions to their building's terrace.

views.says: Say 'turn left at the stairs'. Everyone understands left and right.
Say 'go to the east side of the stairs'. Left changes when you turn round.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence. For Revathi: in the left-right test, 'turn right' worked only from one start, but east worked every time. For Anu: most people do not know which way east is inside a building, and someone walking up the stairs always faces the same way, so 'left' works there.
items.why: Both sisters have a point. East works for any reader. Left works when everyone arrives facing the same way.

items.p: In the coin test, why is it fair to hide the coin away from all furniture?
items.a: If the coin is next to the bed, the finder can just look for 'next to the bed' on any map. In open floor, only a map with the right distances shows where it is.
items.why: A strong answer says how a landmark next to the coin would let a bad map look good.

items.p: A memory map shows the cupboard as big as the bed. Really, the cupboard is half as long. What will a finder using this map probably do?
opts: Go to exactly the right spot
Miss the spot, because the gaps around the cupboard are wrong
items.why: If one thing is drawn too big, the gaps next to it are squeezed or stretched, so an X near it is in the wrong place.

items.p: Put the steps of making a tile map in order.
items: Draw each piece of furniture where you counted it
Count the tiles along each wall
Draw the walls on squared paper, one square per tile
Count tiles from the walls to each piece of furniture
Add a north arrow and a key
a: Count the tiles along each wall
Draw the walls on squared paper, one square per tile
Count tiles from the walls to each piece of furniture
Draw each piece of furniture where you counted it
Add a north arrow and a key
items.why: The walls come first, because everything else is counted from them.

items.p: A grown-up and a child each map a room in their own steps. The child's map has more squares, so it must be wrong.
items.why: False. The child's steps are shorter, so there are more of them. Both maps shrink every wall by the same amount, so both have the same shape and both are right.

items.p: In the left-right test, chit A said 'forward, then right'. It found the coin only when you started facing east. Why that wall?
items.a: Chit A was written by someone facing east. It works only for someone standing the same way, because forward and right turn with your body.
items.why: A strong answer links the one start that worked with the way the writer was facing.

items.p: You face south. Which way is your right hand pointing?
items.why: Facing south, west is on your right and east is on your left. It is the mirror of facing north. Stand up and try it.

items.p: Draw a map of your bedroom from above. Include a key with at least four symbols and a north arrow.
items.a: A box for the room with gaps for the door and window, symbols for the bed, cupboard and other things, a key that explains every symbol, and an N arrow.
items.why: A strong map shows things from above, explains every symbol, and shows north so the reader can turn it.

items.p: Holding a map so that its north arrow points to the real north is called ____ the map.
items.why: When a map is set, every place on it lies the same way as the real place.

items.p: The Sun rises a little north of east in June and a little south of east in December. Is the morning Sun still good enough for finding east for a home map? Why?
items.a: Yes. It is only a little off, so it shows which wall is roughly east. For a home map, the closest wall is all we need. For a ship at sea, you would need a compass.
items.why: A strong answer says how big the error is compared with what the map needs.

items.p: Sort these directions. Do they depend on which way you face, or are they fixed to the Earth?
items.a: see items
items.why: Body directions turn when you turn. Earth directions stay put.

items.p: On a map, 1 square stands for 10 steps. The shop is 4 squares from your gate. About how many steps is that?
items.why: Each square is 10 steps, so 4 squares is 4 times 10, which is 40 steps.

items.p: A desert ant lives in the hot Sahara. She must find food far from her nest and get home before the heat kills her. How does counting her steps help her?
items.a: Smell trails do not work well on hot, windy sand. By counting her steps, and using the Sun for direction, she knows how far and which way her nest is. So she can run straight home instead of searching.
items.why: A strong answer says her problem first, the heat and far trips, and then how counting steps solves it.

items.p: On every map in history, north has been at the top.
items.why: False. North at the top is a custom. Al-Idrisi's famous world map of 1154 had south at the top.

items.p: In the story Thatha and the Six Towers, Meenakshi drew a map for her grandfather. Why did he walk the wrong way, even though her first map showed every tower?
opts: When he turned round, the map did not turn with him, so left and right swapped
items.why: Her first map had no direction arrow, so he did not know how to turn it. After she added an east arrow, he could turn the map to match the ground.

items.p: A family is deciding how to get to a new friend's house in Mysuru.

views.says: Use the phone map. It shows exactly where we are.
Ask the friend for landmarks: the temple, the big banyan tree, the blue gate. Landmarks never run out of charge.
Draw our own map from the friend's directions, so we can look at it any time.

items.ask: Which way would you choose? Give a reason. Then say one good point from another person.
items.a: A strong answer picks one way with a reason and fairly gives another view. For example, the phone map is exact, but a phone can run out of charge or lose signal. Landmarks are easy to remember. A drawn map needs the distances to be roughly right.
items.why: Each way has real strengths and weaknesses. A strong answer weighs them.

items.p: Your tile map had no colours, no cushions and no smells, yet it found the coin. What did it keep that made it work?
items.a: It kept where things are, how far apart they are, and which way they lie. Those are what a finder needs. Colours and smells do not help you find a spot on the floor.
items.why: A strong answer names distance and direction, and says why the other things do not matter for finding a place.

items.p: In the 1700s, mapmakers in Europe argued about California.

views.says: Many good maps show California as an island. So many maps cannot all be wrong.

views.who: Eusebio Kino, a priest who travelled there
views.says: I went there over land and saw no sea. The land carries on to the west.

items.ask: Who would you believe, and why? Then say why the other person's view made sense at the time.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Kino, because he checked the real place, while the maps were copies of each other. It also says the mapmaker's view made sense, because many maps agreeing looks like good evidence when you cannot go there yourself.
items.why: The heart of the story: copies do not count as extra evidence. Only checking the real place does.

items.p: You walk north and keep going, over land and ice, until you reach the North Pole. Which way is everything around you now?
items.why: At the North Pole, every direction leads away from the pole, so every direction is south. There is no further north to go.

items.p: Nain Singh Rawat mapped the road to Lhasa in the 1860s by counting his steps on a string of 100 beads. Why do you think he used beads instead of just counting in his head?
items.a: Counting thousands of steps in your head is easy to lose. Moving one bead for each 100 steps keeps the count safe, even if you are tired or talking to someone.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a long count needs a record that does not depend on memory.

items.p: Draw a map of a room where 'forward 2 tiles, then right 3 tiles' and '2 tiles north, then 3 tiles east' lead to the same tile. Mark which way the walker must face at the start.
items.a: A grid with the start, the coin 2 tiles north and 3 east, and an arrow showing the walker faces north at the start.
items.why: The two sets agree only if the walker starts facing north, because then forward is north and right is east.

items.p: Arun's map says 1 square is 10 steps. His sister draws the same street with 1 square for 5 steps. Whose map of the street is bigger on paper?
items.why: Her squares stand for fewer steps, so she needs twice as many squares for the same street. Her map is twice as long and twice as wide, but the same shape.

items.p: Some people think more detail always makes a better map. Do you agree? Give an example from your own maps.
items.a: Not always. My street map would be too crowded if I drew every auto and every flowerpot. A good map shows what the reader needs, such as roads and landmarks, and leaves the rest out.
items.why: A strong answer tests the popular belief with an example and says what a map should keep.

items.p: Two people can draw two different maps of the same place, and both can be correct.
items.why: True. A map for a visitor shows the route and landmarks. A map for a plumber shows the pipes. Both are right about what they show.

items.p: Put these in order of how big a piece of the world the map shows, from smallest to biggest.
items.why: Each map takes in a bigger area than the one before it, so each one has to shrink the real place more.

items.p: A compass needle is a small magnet. Why does it point north and south?
opts: The Earth acts like a giant magnet and turns the needle
items.why: The Earth is magnetic, so a free magnet turns to line up north and south. You will learn more about this in the unit on compasses.

items.p: A desert ant on stilts walked past her nest. An ant with shortened legs stopped too soon. Why do both results point to the same answer?
items.a: Both ants took their usual number of steps. Longer steps carried one ant too far, and shorter steps left the other short. So both were counting steps, not looking for the nest.
items.why: A strong answer explains that the two opposite results both fit one idea: counting steps.

items.p: Chennai is on the east coast of India, and Kochi is on the west coast. You fly from Chennai to Kochi. Which way do you go?
items.why: Kochi is on the west coast and Chennai on the east, so you travel roughly west, across the country.

items.p: Scientists found cells in a rat's brain that fire in a grid pattern as the rat moves around. Why might a brain need something like a grid?
items.a: A grid lets the brain keep track of how far and which way the rat has gone, like squares on a tile map. Then the rat can find the way back, even in the dark.
items.why: A strong answer links the brain's grid to measuring distance and direction, as on a tile map.

items.p: The lines that mark borders between Indian states can be seen on the ground from an aeroplane.
items.why: False. Borders are drawn by people on maps. On the ground there is usually no line. Sometimes a river or hills run along a border.

items.p: Design a map symbol for each of these: a school, a hospital, a temple and a bus stop. Then draw a key for them.
items.a: Four simple symbols, each easy to draw small and different from the others, and a key naming each one.
items.why: A strong symbol is simple, easy to draw small, and cannot be mixed up with another one.

applications: Phone maps use GPS satellites to find where you are. Gladys West's careful maths on the exact shape of the Earth helped make GPS accurate.

In the 1950s, Marie Tharp drew the first maps of the floor of the Atlantic Ocean from depth measurements taken by ships. She found a long valley running down the middle of an underwater mountain range.
Auto, taxi and delivery drivers use maps to reach addresses they have never visited.
Pilots and sailors steer by compass directions, because at sea or in the sky there is no left turn at the temple.
Architects draw a plan of a flat from above before it is built, with every room to scale.
Fire exit maps in malls and hospitals show the way out, with a red dot marking 'you are here'.
Farmers and village offices keep land maps that show where each field begins and ends.
The Survey of India, started in 1767, makes the official maps of the country.
Rescue teams after floods and cyclones use maps to plan which roads are still open.

open_questions.q: How exactly do birds such as Arctic terns find their way across whole oceans?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know birds use the Sun, the stars, smells and the Earth's magnetism. But how a bird senses magnetism, and how they put all these clues together, is still argued about.

open_questions.q: How does the brain turn signals from grid cells into the feeling of knowing where you are?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can record grid cells and place cells firing. Nobody yet knows how these signals become the sense of 'I am in my kitchen'.

open_questions.q: Why do some people find their way easily and others get lost often?
open_questions.why_open: Practice, attention and the way someone learned to give directions all seem to matter. Scientists are still finding out how much each one counts.

jokes.a: Don't worry, I'm pointing you in the right direction.

jokes.j: Why was the map so calm?
