jokes.j: Why did the student bring a ladder to geography class?
jokes.a: She wanted to see the bird's-eye view.

jokes.j: Which direction do ants like most?
Why did the tile map win the treasure hunt?
What did the east say to the west?
Why don't maps ever get bored?
jokes.a: There's always something new around the corner.

jokes.j: What did one map say to the other?
jokes.a: You've got everything I need, to scale.

jokes.j: Why did the compass needle never tell a lie?
jokes.a: It always pointed true north. Well, nearly.

jokes.j: Why did the desert ant wear stilts?

jokes.j: Why did the map love idli and sambar?
jokes.a: It was the usual route to breakfast.

jokes.j: Why did the bed refuse to go on the memory map?

jokes.j: How does a map say thank you?
Why did the Sun get up early every morning?
jokes.a: Someone had to show us where east was.

jokes.j: Why did the island of California vanish?
What did the lost auto driver say to his phone?
jokes.a: Please, just tell me which way is east.

maths.problem: Lakshmi made a tile map of her room. The room is 8 tiles long and 6 tiles wide. How many tiles cover the whole floor?
maths.explain: The floor has 6 rows, and each row has 8 tiles. 6 times 8 is 48.
maths.context: This is about the tile map from the coin test, where one floor tile is one square on paper.
maths.why_maths: Counting rows of equal size tells you the number of tiles without counting each one.

maths.problem: On Meenakshi's map, 1 square is 10 steps. From the gate to the temple is 2 squares, the temple to the water tank 6 squares, and the water tank to Tower D 9 squares. How many steps is it from the gate to Tower D?
maths.explain: 2 + 6 + 9 = 17 squares. Each square is 10 steps, so 17 times 10 is 170 steps.
maths.context: This is about the story Thatha and the Six Towers, where Meenakshi drew a map with 1 square for every 10 steps.
maths.why_maths: The scale turns squares on paper back into real steps, so you can plan a walk before you take it.

maths.problem: A treasure is 3 squares north and 4 squares east of the door on a grid. Ravi says, 'Then it is 4 squares east and 3 squares north.' Is he right?
maths.explain: Going 3 north then 4 east, or 4 east then 3 north, ends on the same square. The order of the moves does not change where you end up, as long as nothing blocks the way.
maths.context: This is about finding a spot on a grid, as in the Tile Treasure game.
maths.why_maths: Seeing that the moves can swap order helps you find the shortest route on any grid.

maths.problem: In the coin test, the memory map was 3, 2 and 4 tiles off in three rounds. The tile map was 0, 1 and 0 tiles off. How many tiles off was each map in total? How many times better was the tile map?
maths.answer: The memory map was 9 tiles off in total. The tile map was 1 tile off. So the tile map was 9 times closer.
maths.context: This is about the coin test, where a finder used each map to put a chit on the hidden coin's tile.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the rounds smooths out lucky guesses, and comparing totals shows how much better one map is.

maths.problem: A child measured a room as 18 steps long and 14 steps wide. A grown-up measured the same room as 13 steps long. About how wide do you think the grown-up found it: 5, 10 or 14 steps? Why?
maths.explain: For the child, the width is a bit less than the length, about 4 steps less out of 18. The grown-up's steps are longer, so both numbers shrink. 10 is a bit less than 13 in the same way. 14 would make the room nearly square, and 5 would make it very thin.
maths.context: This is about the Child Steps, Grown-up Steps test, where two people measure the same room with their own feet.
maths.why_maths: If both maps have the same shape, you can predict one person's count from the other's.

roots.context: We have drawn maps of a room, a home and a street, and tested which map finds a hidden coin. Now we ask what a map tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your tile map had no colours, no cushions and no smells. Yet it led someone straight to the coin. It kept only how far apart things are, and which way they lie. So a map can be true about a place while looking nothing like it.
deep_truth.habit: We think a true picture must look like the thing it shows, like a photo. But a map is true in a different way. It keeps the distances and directions between things, and drops almost everything else.
deep_truth.evidence: In the coin test, the plain tile map led the finder to the right tile, while the memory map, with its guessed distances, was tiles off. In the child-and-grown-up test, two maps of different sizes had the same shape, and both were right.

three.who_am_i: You carry a map of your home inside you. That is how you find the bathroom in the dark.
three.what_is_life: A desert ant keeps her own map by counting her steps and watching the Sun. That is how she gets home alive across hot sand.
three.what_is_this_world: The ground has no lines for borders or street names. People draw those, but the hills and rivers were there first.

roots.thread: One room can have many true maps: your tile map, your grandmother's map in her head, an ant's count of steps, a plumber's plan of the pipes. They look nothing alike. Each one keeps a different part of how the room is arranged, and each one works for the one who uses it. The room is one, and the maps are many.

teachings.source: Alfred Korzybski, Science and Sanity (1933), page 58
teachings.teaching: A map is not the land it shows. But if the map is correct, it has the same arrangement as the land, and that is why it is useful.
teachings.link: This is what the coin test showed. The tile map was not the room, but every distance on it matched the room's arrangement. That is why it found the coin.

teachings.source: Jorge Luis Borges, 'On Exactitude in Science' (1946)
teachings.teaching: In this very short story, mapmakers in an empire made a map as big as the empire itself, matching it point for point. The next people found it useless and left it to rot in the desert.
teachings.link: A map helps because it is smaller than the place and leaves things out. Your tile map fitted on one page, so you could see the whole room at once.

teachings.source: Majjhima Nikaya 22, the Alagaddupama Sutta (the parable of the raft)
teachings.teaching: The Buddha said his teaching is like a raft for crossing a river. When you reach the other bank, you do not carry the raft on your head. You leave it and walk on.
teachings.link: A map is the same kind of tool. It is for getting somewhere, such as from the door to the coin. Once Thatha knew the way home, he hardly needed the map.

science.text: In 1971, John O'Keefe found 'place cells' in rats' brains, which fire when the rat is in one particular spot. In 2005, May-Britt Moser and Edvard Moser found 'grid cells', which fire in a grid pattern as the rat moves. The three shared the Nobel Prize in 2014.
Desert ants measure distance by counting steps. Ants given stilts walked past their nest.
How signals from these cells become the feeling of knowing where you are is not known.

other_view.view: No map is simply true. Every map leaves things out, and the mapmaker chooses what. A city map for cars can leave out the footpaths that walkers need. So instead of asking whether a map is true, we should ask what it is for and whom it leaves out.

practice.title: Walk the map with your eyes closed
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Picture your bed. Now picture walking from your bed to the kitchen. Count the steps in your head. Which way do you turn at each door? Open your eyes. Now walk it for real and count. Was the map in your head right?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat. The coin test needs only squared paper, a coin and a family member. It works best with square floor tiles, which most Indian flats have. Without tiles, heel-to-toe steps work, with a little more error. The coin is hidden in open floor, away from furniture, because a coin next to the bed is easy to find with any map. With the coin in open floor, a memory map is usually 2 to 4 tiles off, and a tile map 0 or 1, so the difference is clear. If it is not, the step says to pick a spot further from furniture. Finding east uses the patch of morning sunlight, never looking at the Sun, and a phone compass or bought compass on a cloudy day or later in the day. The left-right test uses tiles instead of steps, because steps differ between people. In the child-and-grown-up steps test, the two maps will be close to the same shape, but not exactly, and the step says so. The balcony activity keeps the child away from the railing. The visitor project needs a grown-up outside the flat. The spine is the bird's-eye view activity, finding the four directions, the coin test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1539, a Spanish sailor named Francisco de Ulloa sailed up the long gulf west of Mexico. At its top, he found that the water ended in land. So California was joined to the rest of North America. But in the early 1600s, some mapmakers in Europe began to draw California as a huge island. A map printed in Amsterdam in 1622 showed it this way. Other mapmakers copied it, often without checking, and the island spread from map to map for about a hundred years. Then Eusebio Kino, a priest born in Italy, travelled for years by horse and on foot across what is now northern Mexico and Arizona. In 1701, from near the place where the Gila River joins the Colorado River, he saw the land carry on, unbroken, to the west. There was no sea there. His map showing California joined to the mainland was printed in Paris in 1705. Even so, some maps kept the island. In 1747, King Ferdinand VI of Spain declared that California is not an island.
how_we_found_out.who: Francisco de Ulloa, a Spanish sailor, and Eusebio Kino, a priest born in Italy who worked in Mexico
how_we_found_out.when: 1539 (Ulloa's voyage), 1622 (an early island map), 1701 to 1705 (Kino's journey and map), 1747 (the Spanish king's order)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Mapmakers in Europe drew California as an island for about a hundred years, copying one another. Kino went there over land and saw that the land was joined to the mainland. A map is only as good as the checking behind it.
